definition: Successive Linear Programming (SLP), also known as Sequential Linear Programming, is an optimization technique for approximately solving nonlinear optimization problems.
details: It is related to, but distinct from, quasi-Newton methods. Starting at some estimate of the optimal solution, the method is based on solving a sequence of first-order approximations (i.e. linearizations) of the model. The linearizations are linear programming problems, which can be solved efficiently. As the linearizations need not be bounded, trust regions or similar techniques are needed to ensure convergence in theory. SLP has been used widely in the petrochemical industry since the 1970s. Since then, however, they have been superseded by sequential quadratic programming methods. While solving a QP subproblem takes more time than solving an LP one, the overall decrease in the number of iterations, due to improved convergence, results in significantly lower running times and fewer function evaluations."

explainer.lead: Successive linear programming approximates nonlinear optimisation problems by solving a sequence of linear programs. It matters because linear programs can be solved efficiently, making hard nonlinear problems tractable.

tiers.eli5: It is like replacing a curvy road with a series of straight stretches so you can plot a route step by step.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers start from an estimate of the optimal solution and solve a sequence of first-order linearisations, using trust regions or similar techniques since linearisations need not be bounded. A pitfall is that convergence is only ensured in theory with such safeguards.
tiers.paperLevel: An optimisation technique for approximately solving nonlinear optimisation problems, related to but distinct from quasi-Newton methods, based on solving a sequence of first-order approximations (linearisations) of the model as linear programming problems.

explainer.example: A nonlinear process model is linearised around the current estimate, the resulting linear program is solved, and the estimate is updated repeatedly.
